newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Olivetti's Caio sees hi-tech future.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Olivetti's Caio sees hi-tech future.

text.p: Olivetti 's embattled chief executive Francesco Caio on Thursday outlined his vision for the future of his crisis-hit company as an integrated hi-tech group linking information technology with telecoms.

He told the influencial upper house Senate industry commission of a new Olivetti linking its core systems and services company with its newer telecoms interests, while seeking partners for personal computers and for office equipment company Lexikon.

"The future of Olivetti is positioned between the business of systems and services and telecommunications. For the other businesses we must find partnerships or alliances," Caio said in his testimony to the Senate commission.

Caio tried to assure long-suffering investors and employees over the future of his struggling loss-making group by emphasising Olivetti did not want or seek state aid, and that it was not planning to close its ailing personal computers business.

But he could not escape admitting that the economic and financial performance of his company was still "strongly negative" and confirmed that Olivetti's loss-making personal computer business would not break-even in 1996 as earlier hoped.

The ongoing problems at Olivetti took a dramatic turn for the worse last week, as it posted poor first-half 1996 results and its director-general in charge of finance and auditing for only two months Renzo Francesconi suddenly resigned and cast his doubts over the accuracy of the group's accounts.

The 39-year-old Caio, only appointed to head Olivetti in early July, triumphed in ousting long-standing chairman Carlo De Benedetti from the board last week, but his task has grown harder as Olivetti's problems have deepened.

Hard on the heels of the Senate hearing came news that the industry commission of Italy's lower house of parliament, the Chamber of Deputies, would start an inquiry next week into Olivetti calling De Benedetti, Caio and new chairman Antonio Tesone forward for questioning.

Meanwhile, Olivetti's board and auditors were meeting stock market watchdog authority Consob Thursday afternoon to try and iron out the seven points that Consob wanted answering over the group's financial accounts.

Against this background, Caio was outlining his future for Olivetti's five companies, ironically coming under questioning by Senator Franco Debenedetti, the brother of Carlo whose tenure of 18-years of chairmanship of Olivetti ended last week.

Caio saw Olivetti focusing on three of its companies to link its system and services, which providing automation systems for banking and retailing with its two telecoms companies Omnitel and Telemedia.
Systems and services had been the backbone of Olivetti, providing 60 percent of sales, but first-half results showed an alarming slide in profit margins as competition hotted up.
Omnitel, where Olivetti has a 41.3 percent stake, and Telemedia which incorporates Olivetti's fixed-line telecoms interests, have yet to make any profits and are absorbing cash.

For Olivetti's other companies, Caio was adamant that Olivetti had no intention of closing its personal computer company and said it was looking for a partner for the business which turned in a loss of 200 billion lire ($131 million) in 1995, and a loss of 10 billion lire in the first half of 1996.

Lexikon, which makes faxes and printers, would look for partners Caio said, but there was no mention of earlier Olivetti plans to float 40 percent of this profitable company on the New York stock market.
